top_comments: I'm getting fatigued with the constant introduction of names and the impenetrability of mapping these brand new names to use cases.I think internally, Google, Anthropic and OpenAI are thinking "It's so easy, you just use Neon for X, Carbon for Y" - but most of the world is trying to map Sol, Astra, Neon, Opus, Fable, Mythos, Carbon, Haiku, etc.I just hope they finally land on a naming scheme they are happy with and just stick with it. But I have my doubts. Perhaps they are all benefiting from this confusion.

Is there any theory on what is Anthropic's secret sauce? I have been using the latest Gemini models and they just don't seem as good as Opus 5.5 despite the benchmarks. Yeah it comparable on some tasks maybe slightly better but as an overall general intelligent model nothing compared to Opus 5.5 and it hard for me to understand why. Opus feels like human level intelligent like I'm talking to a coworker basically while GPT and Gemini feel like I'm talking to an AI and have to change how I talk. It hard to explain and maybe I'm the only one that feels this.Is it because Anthropic put a ton more effort into the character of the model that it basically roleplays as a human and that why it tends to think better when giving tasks that it might not be trained heavily on.I have used Carbon more than most model to try and get the same results but it just feels like i'm talking to a smart AI. Which is fine if you are asking questions, researching an idea, but if you actually want to work on something, build something, it just falls apart. Like Opus can run for days on a task and it feels like it understand what it was doing 2 days ago even when it might not be in it context while other models feel like they breakdown and get lost or falter as the task grows.

Something that is interesting is how it's positioned in the overall fleet of Gemini models. Although overall more Intelligent than Carbon, Carbon is still positioned as the 'long horizon' model. This is clear on AA Index, where we see higher overall scores for Neon but lower scores in evals like CritPt which test research-scale reasoning capabilities.With the frontier getting more jagged, we might see more of this 'less intelligent overall but useful for the frontier tasks'-type models, meaning picking a model will only get more difficult from here.(FD: I work at AA)

top_comments: It's interesting how the first period of AI companies was improving their AIs and now they are diversifying into just about every other industry with models that they withhold from the market. Effectively these companies are now competing with each and every one of their customers whilst having the inside scoop on what those customers are up to.To me this signifies two things: the low hanging fruit has been plucked and we are now on the slow but steady incremental improvement part of the trajectory and the second is that if you share your corporate secrets with these companies you can count on that being used against you sooner or later and they'll be using tools that you can't buy from them at any price.

Naming the chip Jalapeño is great. Not only does it play into hot potato chips, but also Jalapeño peppers come from Xalapa, a city in Mexico. Xalapa comes from the Nahuatl word Xallapan, which roughly translates to "place of sandy water." These chips are made from quartz sand, and a data center then uses water to cool them. A data center is a place of sandy water!

I am seeing good results with chip design by treating it as a software design problem, using the agent to write software to generate my circuits and then write software to automate my EDA flow. Then the agent can babysit my several runs of multi hour simulation so I don't have to anymore.I don't drive straight at the RTL though. Infact only a small fraction of the design in RTL, the bulk is analog.
